newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: French ministers chided for rushed Guiana visit.
newsitem.headline: French ministers chided for rushed Guiana visit.

text.p: Politicians in French Guiana have criticised the rushed arrival of two cabinet ministers from Paris in response to recent organised riots that followed student protests in the French overseas territory.

"They (the ministers) arrived just like that in the early hours (of Tuesday) without consulting anyone, while we were working for their official arrival with extremely serious sessions to propose concrete solutions," Antoine Karam, president of French Guiana's Regional Council, told reporters.

The headquarters building of the council was attacked and burned with firebombs on November 8, the first of four nights of riots in French Guiana's capital Cayenne. Damage has been estimated at more than $2 million.

"French Guiana has had enough of being behind in development. Being simultaneously institutionaly a first world country and at the same time a third world country in many respects. We continue to launch rockets...in the background of slums. It is unacceptable," Karam said.
The European Space Agency (ESA) Ariane launch centre in Kourou, French Guiana, has been untouched by the riots.

French Guiana lags behind mainland France in housing, education and health. The official unemployment rate exceeds 23 percent of the workforce and young people under 25, who make up 50 percent of the population, are the hardest hit.
A general strike has been called for Wednesday by one of French Guiana's largest labour unions.

France's education minister, Francois Bayrou, and its overseas territories minister, Jean-Jacques de Perretti, arrived early on Tuesday on a visit which had been expected to take place "in the next several weeks," surprising local officials.
"We are here to listen to all of (French) Guianese society. Our method is to listen with respect...I haven't arrived with prefabricated solutions," Bayrou said.

The riots were sparked by a strike of high school students protesting the poor conditions in local schools. Protests were soon overtaken by more radical groups, some of whom favour French Guiana's independence from Paris.
Paris has sent more than 500 paramilitary riot police reinforcements to this city of 35,000.

One person died and at least 20 were injured during four nights of rioting last week in Cayenne. The violence caused millions of dollars in damage to property -- mostly government buildings and shops.
Pierre Dartout, the French administrator known by the title prefect in Guiana, described the riots as being "planned actions by organised groups who aim to destabilise Guiana."
Though he had no evidence that foreign goverments were to blame, he said many of the rioters were foreign nationals.
Illegal immigrants, mostly from Haiti, Brazil and neighbouring Surinam make up about a quarter of the population of 150,000. More than 8,000 of the total population receive French welfare payments.
The immigrants were lured to French Guiana during a growth period in the late 1980s and early 1990s, triggered in part by construction at the ESA launch centre and public works projects.
French Guiana, located in northern South America and in French hands since the 17th century, is the only non-independent territory on the continent.
